Many BERT-based embedders stop at 512 tokens, and libraries often truncate longer chunks silently. Compare sizes at a fixed token budget: top 10 small chunks against top 2 large ones.

question: Why combine embeddings with keyword search?
answer: Because they fail differently: embeddings match paraphrase but miss rare exact strings like error codes and part numbers, while BM25 matches those tokens and misses paraphrase. Hybrid search fuses both rankings, usually with a reranker on top.
explanation: Combine embeddings with keyword search because they fail on different queries: embeddings match meaning and paraphrase but blur rare exact strings, while BM25 matches exact tokens but misses synonyms. Hybrid search runs both retrievers and fuses their ranked lists into one.

An embedding model splits "E-4012" into subword pieces and compresses the passage into one vector, so one rare token barely moves it; BM25 weights it heavily because few documents contain it. Reciprocal rank fusion scores each document Σ 1/(k + rank), with k = 60 by convention. If BM25 ranks D1, D2, D3 and embeddings rank D3, D1, D4, D1 scores 1/61 + 1/62 ≈ 0.0325, D3 0.0323, D2 and D4 about 0.016.

Why fuse ranks, not scores? BM25 scores have no fixed scale and vary by query, while cosine similarities sit between −1 and 1, so adding them needs normalization and tuning; RRF (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009) needs neither. A cross-encoder reranker then rescores the top candidates. Hybrid helps most with IDs, code and jargon, and out of domain, where the BEIR benchmark (2021) found BM25 a robust zero-shot baseline.

question: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
answer: Retrieval and generation separately. Retrieval: recall@k and nDCG on labelled question-document pairs. Generation: faithfulness (every claim supported by the context), relevance and citations. Many bad answers are retrieval failures.
explanation: Evaluate a RAG system in two stages: whether retrieval finds the passages that contain the answer, then whether the generated answer is faithful to them and on topic. Faithfulness means every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, which differs from correctness against the truth.

Toy eval: Q1 has 2 relevant chunks, both in the top 5; Q2 has 1, ranked 7th; Q3 has 3, two in the top 5; Q4 has 1, ranked 1st. Recall@5 is 1, 0, 0.67 and 1, a mean of 0.67; the hit rate is 3/4. For generation, split an answer into claims and check each against the context: 3 of 4 supported is faithfulness 0.75, the RAGAS ratio (Es et al., 2023).

Interviewers ask where labels come from: real user questions with expert-marked passages beat LLM-written ones, which are easier. Label document spans, not chunk IDs, or re-chunking breaks the eval set, and spot-check LLM judges against humans. Watch crossed cases: an answer can be correct but unfaithful, from model memory, or faithful but wrong because the source is outdated.

question: What actually reduces hallucinations?
answer: Grounding, not scolding: retrieval with citations, permission to answer that it does not know, tool calls for facts and arithmetic, and a verification pass. The model optimises for the likeliest next token, not for truth, so instructions alone will not.
explanation: Hallucinations drop when the model is grounded and checked: retrieval with citations, tools for facts and arithmetic, permission to say "I don't know", and a verification pass. A hallucination is fluent output that the source or the world does not support. Next-token prediction rewards plausible text, not true text, so instructions alone barely help.

Kalai et al., "Why Language Models Hallucinate" (2025), argue that training and benchmarks reward guessing. Score 1 for right and 0 for wrong or "I don't know": a model 30% sure expects 0.3 from guessing, 0 from abstaining, so it guesses. With a 1-point penalty for errors, the expected score is p − (1 − p), so guessing pays only above 50% confidence; a penalty of t/(1 − t) sets the threshold at t.

Interviewers ask why each fix works: citations make claims checkable against text, and a calculator replaces memory with computation. Lower temperature cuts randomness, not confident errors. RAG still hallucinates when retrieval misses, so give a no-answer path. SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023) flags facts that vary across sampled answers.

question: Why is a bigger context window not always the answer?
answer: Tokens cost money and latency, and accuracy sags for material buried mid-prompt. Retrieving the 2k tokens that matter usually beats pasting 200k. Long windows are for genuinely long documents; prompt caching makes a stable prefix cheaper, not free.
explanation: A bigger context window is not always the answer: every extra token adds cost and latency, and models use facts buried mid-prompt less reliably than facts near the start or end. The context window is the maximum number of tokens, prompt plus output, a model handles per call.

Pasting a 200,000-token manual into every question sends 100 times the input of retrieving the 2,000 tokens that matter: at 10,000 questions a day, 2 billion input tokens versus 20 million. Time to first token grows with prompt length too. In "Lost in the Middle" (Liu et al., TACL 2024), GPT-3.5-Turbo given 20 documents did worse with the answer mid-context than with no documents at all.

Long context fits tasks that need the whole document, such as summarizing a contract or reasoning across a codebase. On prompt caching: a cached prefix skips recomputation and is billed at a discount, but new tokens still attend over it and it still fills the window. Passing a needle-in-a-haystack test, one literal lookup, does not prove a model reasons over all it holds.

question: Prompt, system prompt, tools: what does each do?
answer: The system prompt sets durable role, rules and output format; the user prompt carries the request; tool definitions are schemas the model can call so your code fetches data or acts. The model never runs a tool itself: your application does, or the provider for hosted tools like web search.
explanation: The system prompt sets standing instructions for a conversation, the user prompt carries each request, and tool definitions describe functions the model may ask your code to run. All reach the model as tokens in one sequence, wrapped in role markers, and models are trained, imperfectly, to rank system instructions above user text.

Example: you define get_weather with a JSON schema for city and date, and a user asks about an umbrella for Oslo tomorrow. The model fetches nothing: it returns a structured call, get_weather with city "Oslo", and stops. Your code calls a weather API, appends the result, 6 mm of rain, as a tool-result message and calls the model again to answer. Tool definitions are input tokens on both calls.

Interviewers then probe trust. A system prompt is not a security boundary: users can often extract it, so keep secrets out and enforce permissions in the code that runs tools. Tool results can carry injected instructions, which is why "The Instruction Hierarchy" (Wallace et al., 2024) trains models to rank system over user over tool output.

question: Why did transformers replace RNNs for most NLP tasks?
answer: Self-attention lets every token weigh every other token in one parallel step, instead of pushing information down a recurrent chain, so long-range dependencies survive and training parallelises. The cost is attention quadratic in sequence length.
explanation: Transformers replaced RNNs because self-attention links any two tokens in one step and processes a whole sequence in parallel, so training scales on GPUs. Each token's query is scored against every key, and the softmax of the scores weights the values: softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V.

An RNN computes hidden states one after another, so a signal from token 1 reaches token 100 through 99 updates. If each scales the gradient by 0.9, only 0.9⁹⁹ ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵ survives; LSTM gates soften this but stay sequential. Per layer, attention costs about n²·d operations and recurrence n·d², so attention is even cheaper whenever sequence length n is below width d.

Attention predates the Transformer: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio added it to an RNN translator in 2014; Vaswani and colleagues dropped the recurrence in 2017. Attention ignores order, so positions must be encoded. At 32,000 tokens each head computes about a billion scores per layer. Generation still runs token by token with a growing KV cache, while an RNN keeps a fixed-size state, so state-space models such as Mamba revisit recurrence.

question: How does BERT differ from a GPT-style model?
answer: BERT is an encoder: bidirectional, trained by masking tokens, so every position sees both sides, which suits classification and embeddings but cannot generate. GPT is a causal decoder trained to predict the next token, which is what enables generation.
explanation: BERT is a bidirectional Transformer encoder trained to fill in masked tokens, while a GPT-style model is a decoder trained to predict each next token from left context. The blocks are nearly identical; the mask and objective differ. Devlin and colleagues introduced BERT in 2018, months after OpenAI's first GPT.

In "the cat sat on the mat", GPT's representation of "sat" sees only "the cat sat"; BERT's sees all six words. A causal mask over n tokens allows n(n + 1)/2 attention pairs, 21 of 36 here. BERT's loss is also sparser: it predicts only the 15% of tokens it selects, about 77 of 512. Of those, 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token and 10% stay unchanged, since [MASK] never appears in fine-tuning. GPT gets a loss at every position.

Why can't BERT generate? It can fill a blank, but has no left-to-right factorization, so writing text needs awkward repeated masking. Why still use encoders? A 110-million-parameter BERT-base fine-tuned for classification or embeddings is fast and cheap. RoBERTa (2019) dropped BERT's second objective, next-sentence prediction, at no loss.

question: When should you build a workflow instead of an agent?
answer: Whenever the steps are known ahead of time. A fixed sequence of model calls and code is cheaper, faster and testable, and you can see which step broke. An agent earns its loop only when the next action depends on intermediate results.
explanation: Build a workflow when you can write the steps down in advance: code fixes the order of model calls and tools, and the model fills in each step. An agent is a model in a loop that picks its next action, a tool call or stopping, from earlier results. Anthropic's 2024 essay "Building effective agents" popularized the split.

Errors compound: at 95% accuracy per step, three steps succeed 86% of the time (0.95³) and ten about 60% (0.95¹⁰), and an agent picks its own step count. It also re-sends its growing transcript each turn: at 2,000 tokens a turn, ten turns send 2k + 4k + … + 20k = 110,000 input tokens. A workflow can test and retry each step alone.

An agent earns its cost when the path is unknowable in advance, such as debugging an unfamiliar codebase. Interviewers then ask about guardrails: step and budget limits, sandboxed tools, human approval for irreversible actions, and logged tool calls. A common confusion: tool calls alone do not make an agent; a workflow can call tools at fixed points.

question: What is an embedding?
answer: A fixed-length vector for text, an image or audio, placed so similar meanings land near each other, which turns search into a nearest-neighbour lookup. Vectors only compare within one model, and closeness is not relevance, hence rerankers.
explanation: An embedding is a fixed-length vector that a trained model assigns to text, an image or audio, so that similar meanings land close together. Closeness is usually cosine similarity, cos θ = a·b / (‖a‖ ‖b‖): 1 for vectors pointing the same way, 0 for perpendicular ones.

With unit-length toy vectors, cosine is just the dot product: the query "how do I get my money back" is (0.8, 0.6, 0), "refund policy" (0.6, 0.8, 0) and "GPU memory limits" (0, 0.6, 0.8). The refund page scores 0.96, the GPU page 0.36. At real sizes, a million 768-dimensional float32 vectors take 3.1 GB, so large collections use approximate nearest-neighbor indexes such as HNSW.

The idea took off with word2vec (Mikolov and colleagues, 2013), where king − man + woman lands near queen. Two models' vectors are not comparable, since each learns its own coordinates; switching models means re-embedding everything. For unit vectors ‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2a·b, so cosine and Euclidean distance rank alike. Closeness is not relevance: "cancel my plan" and "upgrade my plan" sit close together.

question: When do few-shot examples beat zero-shot prompting?
answer: When the output format or labelling rule is easier to show than to describe: examples let the model infer the pattern in context, with no weight updates. They cost tokens on every call and can bias style, so add them where an eval shows a gain.
explanation: Few-shot examples beat zero-shot prompting when the output format or labeling rule is easier to show than to describe, such as a house style or where borderline cases belong. Few-shot prompting puts solved input-output pairs in the prompt; the model infers the pattern in context. The GPT-3 paper (Brown and colleagues, 2020) defined the zero-, one- and few-shot settings.

Examples also carry biases. Zhao and colleagues ("Calibrate Before Use", 2021) found GPT-3 favors labels frequent in the examples and labels near the end of the prompt: with four sentiment examples ordered positive, positive, positive, negative, nearly 90% of its predictions were negative. Cost repeats per call: five 150-token examples add 750 input tokens to every request.

Interviewers next ask how to choose examples: cover every label and edge case, balance and shuffle them, or retrieve the nearest ones per input. Min and colleagues (2022) found random labels in demonstrations often barely hurt, so examples teach format and label space more than the mapping, though not for every task. With hundreds of labeled examples, fine-tuning is cheaper per call.

question: What does RLHF change about a base model?
answer: Behaviour, not knowledge. Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, then a reward model trained on human preference pairs, then policy optimisation against it with a KL penalty to stay near the SFT model. DPO skips the reward model.
explanation: RLHF changes how a base model behaves, not what it knows: a model that continues any text becomes an assistant that follows instructions and writes answers people prefer. RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, tunes the model toward a learned score of human preference.

A reward model, scoring the preferred answer r₁ and the rejected one r₂, treats σ(r₁ − r₂) as the probability people prefer the first, so scores of 2.0 and 0.5 give σ(1.5) ≈ 0.82 and a loss of −ln 0.82 ≈ 0.20. PPO then maximizes r(x, y) − β·log(π(y|x) / π_SFT(y|x)), reward minus a KL penalty against the supervised fine-tuned model. In InstructGPT (Ouyang and colleagues, 2022), labelers preferred a 1.3B RLHF model to 175B GPT-3.

Without the KL term the policy games the reward model with long, flattering or repetitive answers: reward hacking. The GPT-4 technical report showed post-training made the pretrained model's well-calibrated probabilities less so. DPO (Rafailov and colleagues, 2023) optimizes the same objective directly on preference pairs, with no reward model or sampling loop. None of these efficiently adds facts.

question: How does byte pair encoding tokenization work?
answer: Text is cut into subword tokens from a fixed vocabulary; BPE builds that vocabulary from characters up, repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair. So common words are one token, rare and non-English text cost more, and letters are invisible.
explanation: Byte pair encoding builds a subword vocabulary by starting from characters or bytes and repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair, until it reaches a target size. Philip Gage published BPE for compression in 1994; Sennrich, Haddow and Birch adapted it to machine translation in 2016.

Toy corpus: low ×5, now ×4, lot ×2. The commonest pair, o w, appears 9 times and becomes ow; then l ow (5) merges into low and n ow (4) into now. Lot stays l, o, t. Encoding replays the merges in order, so unseen town becomes t + ow + n. GPT-2 starts from all 256 bytes, so no input is unknown, and adds 50,000 merges and an end-of-text token: 50,257 tokens.

A bigger vocabulary shortens sequences but enlarges the embedding table: GPT-2 small's 50,257 × 768 matrix holds 38.6 million weights. The same text can need up to 15 times more tokens in one language than another (Petrov and colleagues, 2023). The model sees token IDs, not letters, so counting letters trips it up. BERT's WordPiece merges by likelihood instead.

question: What is the KV cache, and why does it cap concurrency?
answer: Attention keys and values for the prefix, cached per layer, so each new token attends over saved state instead of recomputing the sequence. The cache grows with batch size, sequence length and layers, so GPU memory rather than compute limits throughput.
explanation: The KV cache stores the attention keys and values of every processed token, so each new token attends over stored state instead of re-running the prefix. It caps concurrency because each request holds its own cache in GPU memory, which runs out before compute.

Per token: 2 (keys and values) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes. Llama 2 7B has 32 layers and 32 KV heads of dimension 128, so at 16 bits: 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 524,288 bytes, 2 GiB per 4,096-token sequence. An 80 GB GPU, after 13.5 GB of weights, fits at most about 30 of them.

Why not cache queries? A past token's query is never reused. Decoding is memory-bound: each step reads the weights and every cache to emit one token per sequence, so throughput grows with batch size until caches fill memory. Fixes: grouped-query attention, which gives Llama 3 8B a quarter of the cache with 8 KV heads; 8-bit cache quantization; and PagedAttention, which allocates the cache in blocks to curb fragmentation.

question: What is DPO?
title: What is DPO (direct preference optimization)?
answer: Direct preference optimization: aligning a language model to human preferences by training directly on pairs of preferred and rejected answers with a simple classification-style loss. It targets the same objective as RLHF without training a separate reward model or running reinforcement learning.
explanation: Rafailov and colleagues showed in 2023 that the KL-regularized objective RLHF optimizes has a closed-form best policy, so the reward can be written in terms of the policy itself: β·log(π(y|x) / π_ref(y|x)). Putting that into the usual preference model gives the DPO loss, −log σ(β × [log-ratio of the preferred answer − log-ratio of the rejected one]), where each log-ratio compares the model being trained with a frozen reference, usually the supervised fine-tuned model.

Example with β = 0.1: at the start the model equals the reference, both log-ratios are 0, and the loss is ln 2 ≈ 0.693. After training raises the preferred answer's log-probability by 2 nats and lowers the rejected one's by 1, the margin is 0.1 × (2 + 1) = 0.3 and the loss falls to −ln σ(0.3) ≈ 0.554.

Follow-ups: β plays the role of RLHF's KL penalty, and a smaller β lets the model drift further from the reference; DPO trains offline on a fixed set of pairs, with no sampling during training, which makes it cheaper and more stable than PPO; Meta used it in Llama 3's post-training; and variants include IPO, KTO, which works from thumbs-up and thumbs-down labels instead of pairs, and ORPO, which drops the reference model.

question: What is LoRA?
title: What is LoRA (low-rank adaptation) fine-tuning?
answer: Low-rank adaptation: a fine-tuning method that freezes a model's weights and learns a small low-rank update for chosen weight matrices, W + BA. It trains a fraction of a percent of the parameters, and the update can be merged into W afterwards, so inference costs nothing extra.
explanation: For a d × k weight matrix W, LoRA learns B (d × r) and A (r × k) with a small rank r such as 8 or 16, scaled by α / r. B starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the base model. Hu and colleagues at Microsoft introduced it in 2021, and it is now the most common parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method; on GPT-3 175B they reported 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and a third of the GPU memory of full fine-tuning.

Example: one 4,096 × 4,096 attention projection holds 16.8 million weights. A rank-8 LoRA update for it trains 8 × (4,096 + 4,096) = 65,536 parameters, 0.39% of the matrix. Because only those are trained, optimizer state and gradients shrink by the same factor.

Follow-ups: QLoRA (Dettmers and colleagues, 2023) keeps the frozen base in 4-bit precision and trains LoRA adapters on top, enough to fine-tune a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU; one base model can serve many swappable adapters, one per task; the original paper adapted only the attention query and value matrices, while today all linear layers are common; and for large domain shifts full fine-tuning can still learn more, though LoRA also tends to forget less of the base model's abilities.

question: What is speculative decoding?
answer: A way to speed up LLM generation: a small draft model proposes several tokens, and the large model checks all of them in one forward pass, keeping the longest accepted run. With the right acceptance rule the output follows exactly the large model's distribution, so it gets faster with no loss in quality.
explanation: Decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic: each step reads all the weights to produce a single token, so scoring several proposed tokens in one pass costs about the same as generating one. Each draft token x is accepted with probability min(1, p(x) / q(x)), where p is the large model's probability and q the draft's; at the first rejection, a replacement token is sampled from the leftover distribution max(0, p − q), renormalized. Leviathan, Kalman and Matias at Google and Chen and colleagues at DeepMind published the method in 2022 and 2023.

Example: if the draft proposes 4 tokens and each is accepted with probability 0.8, the large model produces on average (1 − 0.8⁵) / (1 − 0.8) ≈ 3.36 tokens per forward pass instead of 1. The real speedup is lower because the draft model's time counts too; the papers report about 2 to 3 times.

It works best when text is predictable, as in code or low-temperature answers, because the acceptance rate drives the gain. Variants avoid a separate draft model: Medusa and EAGLE add small prediction heads to the large model, and prompt lookup decoding drafts by copying n-grams that already appear in the prompt.

question: What is LLM-as-a-judge?
answer: Using a strong language model to grade outputs, either scoring one answer against a rubric or picking the better of two. It scales the evaluation of open-ended text, where exact-match metrics fail, but the judge has biases you have to measure against human labels.
explanation: The common formats are single-answer grading, pairwise comparison and grading against a reference answer. Zheng and colleagues, who built MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, reported in 2023 that GPT-4's verdicts agreed with human experts over 80% of the time, about as often as the experts agreed with each other. That is why judges are now standard for comparing prompts, models and RAG pipelines during development.

Example: before trusting a judge, compare it with human labels on a sample. On 200 answer pairs, humans prefer A in 140 and the judge picks A in 150, and they agree on 170, which is 85%. But a judge that always said A would already agree 70% of the time, so compute Cohen's kappa: chance agreement is 0.7 × 0.75 + 0.3 × 0.25 = 0.60, and κ = (0.85 − 0.60) / (1 − 0.60) ≈ 0.63.

Known biases: position bias, preferring the first answer shown; verbosity bias, preferring longer answers; and self-enhancement, preferring outputs from its own model family. Mitigations: run each pair in both orders, give a specific rubric, ask for the reasoning before the score, and judge with a different model family from the ones being compared.

question: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
answer: Prompting a model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer, either by showing worked examples or by adding an instruction such as "Let's think step by step". It improves accuracy on multi-step problems such as arithmetic and logic, at the cost of more output tokens.
explanation: Wei and colleagues at Google introduced it in 2022 with few-shot prompts whose examples included the reasoning, not just the answers. The gains appeared mainly in large models; in small ones the written reasoning was often wrong. Kojima and colleagues then showed the same year that a single sentence, "Let's think step by step", gets much of the effect with no examples, which became known as zero-shot chain of thought.

The numbers that made it famous: on the GSM8K grade-school math benchmark, PaLM 540B went from 17.9% with standard prompting to 56.9% with chain of thought. Self-consistency (Wang and colleagues, 2022), which samples several reasoning chains and takes a majority vote on the final answer, raised it to about 74%. Zero-shot chain of thought took InstructGPT from 17.7% to 78.7% on the MultiArith benchmark.

Follow-ups: reasoning models such as OpenAI's o1 and DeepSeek-R1 are trained with reinforcement learning to produce long chains on their own, so explicit prompts help them less; the written chain is not guaranteed to reflect how the model actually reached its answer (Turpin and colleagues, 2023); and the extra tokens add latency and cost.

question: What are the Chinchilla scaling laws?
answer: For a fixed compute budget, a language model's size and its number of training tokens should grow in equal proportion, which works out to roughly 20 training tokens per parameter. Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind showed in 2022 that most large models of the time were too big and undertrained.
explanation: Scaling laws describe how loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute. Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI (2020) concluded that extra compute should go mostly into bigger models. Hoffmann and colleagues trained over 400 models, from 70 million to more than 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, and found that parameters and tokens should each grow with the square root of compute.

Training compute is about 6 × N × D floating-point operations for N parameters and D tokens. Gopher, 280B parameters on 300B tokens, used about 5.0 × 10²³. Chinchilla, 70B parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens (20 per parameter), used a similar 5.9 × 10²³, yet beat Gopher on most benchmarks, including MMLU, 67.5% against 60.0%, at a quarter of Gopher's size, which also makes it cheaper to serve.

The interview nuance: Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute, not total cost. A model served to millions of users pays for its size on every request, so it pays to train a smaller model far longer: Llama 3 8B saw 15 trillion tokens, about 1,900 per parameter. The open question now is data, since high-quality text is finite.

question: What is a mixture of experts (MoE) model?
answer: A model whose feed-forward layers are split into many expert networks, with a router that sends each token to only a few of them. Total parameters can grow without a matching rise in compute per token, so an MoE model gets more capacity for a given inference cost.
explanation: In each MoE layer a small gating network scores the experts for every token, picks the top k, often 1 or 2, and combines their outputs weighted by the router's scores. Attention and embeddings stay shared. Shazeer and colleagues brought sparsely gated experts to large networks in 2017, and the Switch Transformer (Fedus and colleagues, 2021) routed each token to a single expert. An auxiliary load-balancing loss stops the router from sending most tokens to a few favorite experts.

Example: Mixtral 8x7B has 8 experts per layer and routes each token to 2. It holds 46.7 billion parameters in total, not 56 billion, because only the feed-forward blocks are duplicated, and it uses about 12.9 billion per token, so it runs at roughly the speed of a 13B dense model. DeepSeek-V3 takes this further with 671 billion parameters, 37 billion active per token.

The catch: every expert has to sit in memory, so memory follows total parameters while compute follows active ones, and spreading experts over GPUs adds communication. Training can be unstable. And experts tend to specialize in token types and syntax more than in topics; Mixtral's authors found little evidence of experts by subject.

question: What is FlashAttention?
answer: An exact implementation of attention that is faster because it never writes the full n × n attention matrix to GPU memory. It computes attention in tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory, using an online softmax, so it moves far less data and its memory use grows linearly with sequence length.
explanation: Standard attention writes the score matrix QKᵀ and its softmax to the GPU's main memory and reads them back, and those transfers, not the arithmetic, dominate the time. FlashAttention, by Tri Dao and colleagues (2022), fuses the steps into one kernel: it loads blocks of queries, keys and values into on-chip SRAM, keeps a running maximum and sum so the softmax can be rescaled block by block, and in the backward pass recomputes attention instead of storing it.

Example: at 8,192 tokens, one head's score matrix has 8,192² ≈ 67 million entries, 134 MB at 16-bit precision, and with 32 heads that is 4.3 GB for a single layer. FlashAttention never stores it. The paper reported GPT-2 training about 3 times faster than the standard implementation.

Interview points: the result is exact, not an approximation like sparse or linear attention; it does slightly more arithmetic, because of recomputation, yet runs faster, which is the lesson of IO-aware algorithms; and compute is still quadratic in sequence length, only memory becomes linear. FlashAttention-2 (2023) improved parallelism, and FlashAttention-3 (2024) targets H100 GPUs, including 8-bit precision.

question: What is grouped-query attention?
answer: An attention variant in which groups of query heads share one key head and one value head. It shrinks the KV cache, and the memory traffic of generating each token, by the group size while keeping quality close to full multi-head attention.
explanation: Multi-head attention gives every query head its own keys and values; multi-query attention (Shazeer, 2019) shares a single key-value head across all of them, which is fastest but loses some quality. Grouped-query attention, from Ainslie and colleagues at Google (2023), sits in between: with 64 query heads and 8 key-value heads, each group of 8 query heads shares one. They also showed an existing multi-head model can be converted by averaging its heads and training briefly, about 5% of the original pretraining compute.

Example: Llama 2 70B has 80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 key-value heads and a head dimension of 128. At 16-bit precision its cache needs 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes per token, 1.25 GiB for a 4,096-token sequence. With 64 key-value heads it would need 10 GiB, eight times as much.

Why share keys and values but not queries? Only keys and values are cached for later tokens, and reading the cache is what limits decoding speed. Most open LLMs now use it, Llama 3 and Mistral among them. DeepSeek-V2's multi-head latent attention goes further, compressing keys and values into a small latent vector.

question: What are BLEU and ROUGE scores?
answer: Metrics that score generated text by its n-gram overlap with reference texts. BLEU, built for machine translation, is precision-oriented: how many of the output's n-grams appear in the references. ROUGE, built for summarization, is recall-oriented: how many of the reference's n-grams the output recovers.
explanation: BLEU (Papineni and colleagues at IBM, 2002) takes the geometric mean of the clipped n-gram precisions for n = 1 to 4 and multiplies it by a brevity penalty, so very short outputs can't score well by being precise. ROUGE (Chin-Yew Lin, 2004) comes in several forms: ROUGE-N counts recalled n-grams, and ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence.

Example: the reference is "the cat sat on the mat" and the output is "the cat sat on mat". Every output word appears in the reference, so unigram precision is 5/5, and 3 of its 4 bigrams match, 0.75. Recall is lower: ROUGE-1 is 5/6 ≈ 0.83 and ROUGE-2 is 3/5 = 0.6. The output is one word short, so BLEU's brevity penalty is e^(1 − 6/5) ≈ 0.82.

The limits come up in interviews: both reward surface overlap, so a correct paraphrase can score low and a fluent wrong answer with the right words can score high, and they correlate poorly with human judgment on open-ended LLM output. Embedding-based scores such as BERTScore, LLM-as-a-judge and task-specific checks are the usual alternatives. Report BLEU with a standard tool such as SacreBLEU, since tokenization changes the number.

question: What is data drift?
answer: A change in the distribution of a model's inputs between training and production, so the live features stop looking like the data it learned from. When P(X) moves but P(y | X) stays the same, it is called covariate shift.
explanation: Data drift is a change in the distribution of the input features, P(X), between the data a model was trained on and the data it scores in production. The learned mapping from inputs to target may still be right, but the model is now asked about regions of feature space it saw rarely or never, where its errors are larger. When P(y | X) stays fixed while P(X) moves, statisticians call it covariate shift.

Example: a credit model is trained on applicants with a median age of 45. A campaign in a student app then brings in a wave of 22-year-olds with short credit histories. How age and history relate to default hasn't changed, but most predictions now fall in a thin corner of the training data, where the model had little to learn from, so overall accuracy drops even though no rule changed.

Detecting it is a two-sample comparison per feature: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test or Jensen-Shannon distance for continuous features, chi-squared or the population stability index for categorical ones, or a classifier trained to tell old rows from new, where an AUC near 0.5 means no drift. The usual follow-up: drift doesn't always hurt. A shift in a feature the model barely uses can be harmless, so alert on measured or estimated performance, not on drift alone.

question: What is concept drift?
answer: A change in the relationship between the inputs and the target, P(y | X), so the same inputs now call for a different prediction. The model's learned rules go stale even when the input data looks unchanged.
explanation: Concept drift is a change in P(y | X), the mapping the model learned. Unlike data drift, the inputs can look exactly as they did in training; what has changed is what they mean for the target. It can be sudden (a new regulation), gradual (tastes shifting over months) or recurring (seasonal patterns).

Example: a fraud model learned that one large gift card purchase is risky and small ones are safe. Fraudsters notice and switch to many $50 purchases. The input distribution barely moves, so a data drift monitor stays quiet, but a $50 gift card purchase that used to be almost always legitimate is now often fraud. The model keeps calling it safe, and recall falls.

Because the inputs may not move, concept drift shows up in the labels: monitor realized performance once ground truth arrives, or compare the live model with one retrained on recent data. The usual fix is retraining on recent data, with a sliding window or weights that favour new examples. Interviewers often want the contrast in one line: data drift changes P(X), concept drift changes P(y | X), and label shift changes P(y).

question: What is model drift?
answer: The decay of a deployed model's performance over time, also called model decay, because the world it scores moves away from the data it learned from. Data drift and concept drift are its usual causes; a broken data pipeline can look the same.
explanation: Model drift is the symptom: accuracy, AUC or error gets worse after deployment. The causes sit underneath it. Data drift means the inputs changed, concept drift means the relationship between inputs and target changed, and data quality problems mean the model is being fed something different from what the pipeline promises.

Example: a churn model launches with an AUC of 0.82 and a year later scores 0.71. Digging in finds three things. A price increase changed who leaves at a given usage level, which is concept drift. A new student plan brought in users unlike any in training, which is data drift. And a renamed plan code now arrives as missing for 8% of rows, which is a bug that no retraining will fix.

So the first step after a drop is separating the causes: check data quality and schema, then input drift, then performance by segment. Interviewers then ask how to catch it early (monitor performance, or estimate it while labels are delayed) and how to respond (fix the pipeline, retrain on recent data, or rethink features). Not all drift hurts the model, and not every drop in performance is drift.

question: What is training-serving skew?
answer: A mismatch between how features are computed for training and how they are computed when the model serves predictions, so the live model sees inputs that differ from what it learned from. It is a pipeline bug, not a change in the world.
explanation: Training-serving skew is a difference between a model's performance or inputs at training time and at serving time caused by the system itself. Common sources: feature logic written twice (a SQL batch job for training, service code for serving), different data sources or time windows, preprocessing applied in one path but not the other, and training data that includes information the live system doesn't have yet.

Example: a model uses "orders in the last 30 days". The training job counts orders in the warehouse, where refunded orders have already been removed. The online service counts orders from the event stream, where refunds arrive days later. Live values run higher than anything comparable in training, and the model systematically overrates active customers. Offline validation looks fine, because it was computed with the training logic.

Prevention: define each feature once and use it in both paths (a shared transformation library or a feature store), log the features actually served and train on those logs, and compare training and serving values for the same entities. Rule #29 of Martin Zinkevich's Rules of Machine Learning at Google says it directly: save the features used at serving time and use them for training.

question: What is the Population Stability Index (PSI)?
answer: A score for how far a variable's distribution has shifted between two samples, usually training and production: bin the variable, then sum (actual% − expected%) × ln(actual% / expected%) over the bins. Below 0.1 is usually read as stable and above 0.25 as a major shift.
explanation: The population stability index comes from credit scoring, where it compares the score distribution of current applicants with the sample the scorecard was built on. Split the variable into bins, often deciles of the expected sample, and sum (a − e) × ln(a / e), where a and e are each bin's share in the actual and expected samples. It is the KL divergence measured in both directions and added, so it is symmetric.

Example with three bins: training shares are 50%, 30% and 20%; this month's are 30%, 40% and 30%. The terms are (0.3 − 0.5) × ln(0.3/0.5) = 0.102, (0.4 − 0.3) × ln(0.4/0.3) = 0.029 and (0.3 − 0.2) × ln(0.3/0.2) = 0.041, so PSI = 0.17: a moderate shift by the usual rule of thumb, worth a look but not an alarm.

Caveats interviewers probe: the 0.1 and 0.25 cut-offs are industry conventions, not a statistical test; the value depends on the binning; an empty bin makes the log undefined, so a small floor is added; and PSI measures how much one variable moved, not whether the model's performance suffered. It is one of several drift measures, next to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and the Jensen-Shannon distance.

question: How do you monitor a model before its labels arrive?
answer: Watch proxies until the ground truth lands: data quality, drift in the inputs and in the predictions, and, for a well-calibrated classifier, an estimate of performance from its own confidence scores. Confirm with realized performance once the labels arrive.
explanation: Many models get their labels late: a loan defaults months after approval, churn is known 30 to 90 days on, fraud chargebacks take weeks. In that gap you can monitor data quality (missing values, schema, ranges), drift in the input features, drift in the prediction distribution, and an estimate of the model's performance.

Performance estimation uses the model's own probabilities. If a binary classifier is well calibrated, a prediction with score p is right with probability p when it predicts positive and 1 − p when it predicts negative. For four predictions scored 0.9, 0.8, 0.3 and 0.6, the expected accuracy is (0.9 + 0.8 + 0.7 + 0.6) / 4 = 0.75. If past batches estimated 0.85, something has changed before a single label is in. The open-source NannyML library implements this as confidence-based performance estimation (CBPE).

The catch: the estimate assumes the model's probabilities still mean what they meant in training. That holds under covariate shift but not under concept drift, where the model is confidently wrong in a way its scores can't reveal. So check calibration on recent labelled data, treat the estimate as an early warning, and compare it with realized performance as labels arrive.

question: What is the difference between batch and online inference?
answer: Batch inference scores many rows on a schedule and stores the predictions for later lookup; online inference scores each request on demand, within a latency budget. Batch is cheaper and simpler, while online can use features from the moment of the request.
explanation: In batch inference a job runs, say, nightly, scores every user or item, and writes the predictions to a table; the product reads them with a lookup. In online (real-time) inference the model sits behind an API and scores each request as it comes in, typically within tens of milliseconds. It is a separate question from online versus batch learning, which is about how the model is trained.

Example: a shop precomputes the top 20 products for each of its 5 million users every night. Serving is a fast key-value read. But a user who signed up an hour ago has no row, and nobody's recommendations reflect what they clicked five minutes ago. Scoring the session online fixes both, at the cost of a service that must return in time and features that must be available in milliseconds.

Choose by how fast the inputs change and how long the product can wait. Batch wastes compute on users who never return and serves stale predictions; online needs low-latency feature serving and makes training-serving skew easier to introduce. Many systems mix the two: batch jobs generate candidates or embeddings, and an online model re-ranks them with fresh context.

question: What is a feature store?
answer: A system that computes, stores and serves machine learning features from one definition: an offline store with the full history for training and a low-latency online store with the latest values for serving. It stops training and serving from drifting apart and lets teams reuse features.
explanation: A feature store has a registry of feature definitions, an offline store (a warehouse or data lake holding every historical value), an online store (a key-value database holding the current value per entity) and jobs that keep the two in sync. Training reads from the offline store and serving reads from the online one, but both come from the same code.

Its key job is point-in-time correctness. To train a churn model on labels dated March 1, the feature "support tickets in the last 30 days" must be the value as of March 1. A plain join with today's table leaks tickets filed after the label date, the model learns from the future, and offline metrics come out too good. The feature store's point-in-time join fetches, for each label, the feature value that was valid at that timestamp.

Uber's 2017 post on its Michelangelo platform popularized the idea; Feast, open-sourced by Gojek and Google Cloud in 2019, is the common open-source option, and the major cloud ML platforms offer managed ones. Interviewers may also ask when you don't need one: a single batch model owned by one team is usually fine with well-kept tables.

question: What is shadow deployment?
answer: Running a new model next to the live one on real production traffic, logging its predictions without acting on them. It tests the model on real inputs, latency and load with no effect on users.
explanation: In a shadow deployment (or shadow mode) a copy of every request, or of a sample of them, goes to the candidate as well as the live model. Only the live model's output is used; the candidate's predictions are logged and compared, first with the live model's and later with the true outcomes when they arrive.

Example: a bank replacing its fraud model runs the new one in shadow for two weeks on 3 million transactions. It learns that the two models disagree on 4% of transactions, mostly small online purchases; that the candidate's 99th-percentile latency is 180 ms against a 100 ms budget; and that one of its features is always null for in-store payments. All three surface before any customer is affected.

Its limits: shadowing can't measure effects that depend on acting on the predictions, such as clicks on recommendations, so that needs a canary release or an A/B test. It doubles inference cost while it runs. And the outcomes it is judged on were shaped by the live model; in fraud, only transactions the live model approved ever get a label. A common order is offline evaluation, shadow, canary, A/B test, full rollout.

question: What is a canary deployment?
answer: Releasing a new model to a small slice of live traffic, say 1 to 5%, watching errors, latency and business metrics, and widening the rollout in steps while they hold. If they don't, traffic goes back to the old model.
explanation: A canary deployment exposes a new version to a small share of real users first, so a bad release hurts few of them and is rolled back quickly. The name comes from the canaries miners carried to detect gas. The new model serves real predictions, unlike in a shadow deployment, so it can catch problems that only appear when the outputs are used.

Example: a rollout goes 1%, 10%, 50%, 100% over a few days, with automatic rollback if the error rate or 99th-percentile latency crosses a threshold. At 1% of 2 million daily requests the canary gets 20,000 requests a day: plenty to catch crashes, timeouts and broken features, but far too few to detect a small change in conversion rate.

That is the difference interviewers look for. A canary is a safety check that catches breakage early; an A/B test is an experiment, with randomized groups and a sample size planned to measure an effect. Related terms: blue-green deployment switches all traffic between two full environments at once, with instant rollback, and sticky routing keeps a user on one model so their experience doesn't flip between versions.

question: What is the cold start problem?
answer: A recommender or personalization model has nothing to go on for new users or new items that have no interaction history yet. The usual fixes use content features, popularity and onboarding questions until enough interactions arrive.
explanation: Collaborative filtering learns from interactions: who clicked, watched or bought what. A new item has no interactions, so it has no useful embedding; a new user has no history to match. A brand-new platform has both problems at once, sometimes called system cold start.

Example: a streaming service uses matrix factorization. A film added today has no ratings, so its latent vector is meaningless and it never ranks high enough to be shown. Because it is never shown, it never collects ratings, and the problem feeds itself. The fix is to start its embedding from metadata (genre, cast, a text embedding of the synopsis) and reserve some traffic for exploring new items, for example with a bandit.

For new users: ask for a few preferences at sign-up, use context such as device, country and referral source, and fall back to what is popular in their segment. Two-tower models help because the item tower can embed a new item from its features alone. Interviewers also ask how you would measure it: report metrics separately for new users and new items, since averages hide them.

question: What is a two-tower model?
answer: A retrieval model with two neural networks, one that embeds the user or query and one that embeds the item, trained so that the dot product of the two embeddings scores relevance. Item embeddings are computed in advance, so millions of candidates can be searched quickly with nearest-neighbour search.
explanation: The user tower takes user features and recent history; the item tower takes item features such as ID, category and text. Both output vectors of the same size, and training on logged interactions pushes the dot product up for pairs that interacted and down for negatives, often the other items in the same batch.

Example: a video platform with 10 million videos runs the item tower offline and stores the vectors in an approximate nearest-neighbour index (FAISS or ScaNN, for example). At request time it runs the user tower once, retrieves the 500 videos with the highest dot product in a few milliseconds, and hands them to a heavier ranking model that scores each user-video pair with richer features. This retrieve-then-rank design is the standard answer in recommender system design interviews.

The trade-off: the two towers only meet at the dot product, so the model can't learn interactions between user and item features. That is why it retrieves candidates rather than producing the final ranking. In-batch negatives over-penalize popular items, which Yi et al. corrected for at YouTube (RecSys 2019). A plus: the item tower can embed a new item from its features, which eases cold start.

question: How do you decide when to retrain a model?
answer: Retrain on a schedule when the data changes steadily and retraining is cheap, or on a trigger when measured or estimated performance falls below a threshold. Drift alone is a weak trigger, because not all drift hurts the model.
explanation: The options are a fixed schedule (daily, weekly, monthly), a trigger from monitoring, or continual updates as new data arrives. To pick a schedule, measure how fast the model decays: train on data up to a cut-off, then score each later month separately. The shape of that curve says how often retraining pays.

Example: backtesting a demand forecast shows a mean absolute percentage error of 12% in the first month after training, 14% in the second and 19% by the fourth. A monthly retrain keeps error near 12 to 14% for the cost of one job a month; weekly retraining would buy little more. A model whose error is flat for a year can be retrained on a trigger instead.

Follow-ups: which window to train on (a sliding window forgets old patterns, an expanding one keeps them); how label delay limits how fresh the training data can be; and how to swap safely, by validating the new model against the current one on recent data before promotion, the champion-challenger setup. Retraining also can't fix a broken pipeline, so rule that out first.

question: Why can a model that wins offline lose in an A/B test?
answer: Offline metrics are computed on logged data that the old system shaped, against a proxy target, while the A/B test measures the real outcome on live users. Selection bias in the logs, a weak proxy, feedback loops and added latency all open a gap.
explanation: An offline evaluation scores a model on historical data with a metric such as AUC or NDCG. An online A/B test randomizes users between the old and new model and measures what the business cares about, such as revenue, retention or watch time. The two disagree more often than people expect.

Example: a new ranking model lifts NDCG by 3% on last month's click logs but lowers revenue per session in the A/B test. The logs only contain items the old model chose to show, so the new model is graded on a biased sample. Clicks reward eye-catching items while revenue needs purchases, so the proxy was wrong. And the larger model added 60 ms to every page, which costs engagement on its own.

What helps: track how well offline gains have predicted online gains across past launches, and trust a metric only as far as that record goes; use counterfactual estimators such as inverse propensity scoring on logs that record how likely each item was to be shown; use interleaving to compare rankers with less traffic; and keep the A/B test as the final word.
